authorisedInInputCountry.note: This is the key nuance for the case file: the Casumo brand does hold an active DGOJ licence for Spain, but it is held by a distinct entity (Casumo Spain PLC) and, per Spanish rules requiring a .es-hosted licensed product, appears tied to the domain casumo.es — not to the investigated target casumo.com. Casumo's own infrastructure (a 'Restricted Country' page reachable from restricted.casumo.com, and a similar notice surfaced on casumo.es for VPN/proxy users) suggests the operator's intent is to route Spanish traffic to the licensed casumo.es product rather than serve Spain from casumo.com. No evidence was found that casumo.com itself is a DGOJ-authorised URL. This could not be confirmed with a live/geo-located fetch from a Spanish vantage point in this investigation — recommended as a concrete follow-up before any enforcement action.

contradictions: The Gibraltar Remote Gaming Licences 126/127 are attributed to 'Jocularis Ltd' in one secondary source (in a Canada-market context) and to 'Recro Limited' in another (in a general-licensing-summary context); which entity currently holds them was not resolved.

'Recro Limited' appears both as a UK Companies House record (no. 06687605, jurisdiction UK) and as a Malta-registered company per a company-data aggregator (no. C77858, jurisdiction Malta) at the same address used by other Casumo-linked Malta entities; it is unconfirmed whether these are the same legal person or two distinct companies sharing a name.

WHOIS data for the casumo.com domain lists registrant organisation 'Casumo Services Limited' with a Sweden (SE) address, which is inconsistent with the Malta-based entities (Keep Limited, Recro Limited) disclosed elsewhere as the operating companies; the WHOIS record also appears dated (2022-2023) and may not reflect the post-rebrand entity structure.

The brand discloses at least four differently-named regional operating entities (Keep Limited for MGA/EU, Jocularis Ltd/Recro Limited for Gibraltar/UK, Casumo Spain PLC for Spain) for what presents to end users as a single brand and largely single global domain — this is consistent with normal multi-jurisdiction igaming corporate structuring, but it also means no single 'operator of casumo.com' can be named with high confidence from public sources alone.

Casumo Spain PLC's active DGOJ Spanish licence appears bound to the domain casumo.es (Spanish law requires licensed operators to host on a .es domain), not to the investigated target casumo.com; the .com brand's own geoblocking pages (restricted.casumo.com; a Restricted Country notice on casumo.es for VPN users) suggest the operator itself treats casumo.com as excluded from the Spanish market, which cuts against treating casumo.com as an active unlicensed channel into Spain absent evidence it is actually reachable from Spanish IPs.

All direct fetches of casumo.com, its terms page, restricted.casumo.com, the MGA register, the UKGC register, the DGOJ operator page, and a Malta company-data site returned HTTP 403; every fact above attributed to these sources is reconstructed from third-party search-indexed snippets and could not be independently confirmed against the primary page content in this investigation.

priority.rationale: Casumo is a large, long-established, multiply-licensed European igaming brand (MGA, UKGC, Gibraltar) with a documented, currently active, DGOJ-licensed Spanish product and entity (Casumo Spain PLC / casumo.es). The specific target under investigation, casumo.com, is the group's international/generic domain, and available (if unverified by direct geo-testing) evidence indicates the operator actively geoblocks/redirects Spanish traffic away from it toward the licensed casumo.es product, rather than targeting Spain from the unlicensed .com. This does not fit the profile of an evasive illegal operator (no mirror-domain rotation found, identifiable regulated corporate group, existing cross-regulator relationships). Residual risk is limited to possible VPN/geoblock-circumvention access by individual Spanish users, which is a materially different and lower-priority enforcement problem than an operator deliberately marketing an unlicensed product into Spain. Recommend a low-cost verification step (a geo-located test of casumo.com from a Spanish IP, and confirmation of the DGOJ-authorised URL list for Casumo Spain PLC) before any resource commitment; escalate only if casumo.com is shown to be actually reachable and being marketed (Spanish-language ads, EUR/local payment rails) to Spanish consumers outside the licensed casumo.es channel.

factors.harmAndExposure: No evidence found of active Spanish-language marketing, EUR-specific promotion, or targeted advertising on casumo.com; the brand's Spanish traffic appears channelled to a separate licensed domain (casumo.es). Traffic volume/targeting from Spain specifically to casumo.com is unknown and unverified.
factors.consumerHarmSeverity: The brand carries a documented history of UK regulatory fines (2018, 2021) for AML and responsible-gambling failures, and recent consumer reviews describe withdrawal delays — but these relate to the regulated UK/international product, not to unlicensed Spanish activity specifically.
factors.legalReachability: High reachability in principle: entities are EU/UK based, named, and cross multiple cooperative regulators (MGA, UKGC, Gibraltar, DGOJ) — a cross-regulator referral is plausible if evidence of Spain-targeting from casumo.com emerges.
factors.actorBehaviorIntent: No mirror-domain rotation, no fake licence-seal pattern, and apparent proactive geoblocking of Spain from the .com property — behavior inconsistent with deliberate evasion of Spanish regulation; the operator instead maintains a parallel licensed channel for that market.
factors.feasibilityCost: Low expected return on enforcement resource: absent confirmation that casumo.com is actually being accessed by, or marketed to, Spanish consumers outside the licensed casumo.es channel, action would likely target geoblock/VPN circumvention by end users rather than operator conduct.
factors.strategicValue: Low deterrent/precedent value versus pursuing genuinely unlicensed, non-EU-regulated operators; going after an MGA/UKGC/DGOJ-regulated group's generic international domain, where a licensed local alternative already exists, offers limited public-interest signal and carries collateral/reputational risk if the geoblocking claim turns out to be accurate.

analystNotes: Every direct WebFetch attempt against casumo.com, its terms page, restricted.casumo.com, the MGA licensee register, the UKGC public register, the DGOJ operator page, and a Malta company-data site returned HTTP 403 in this session; all facts above are therefore reconstructed from WebSearch-indexed snippets of those pages and from third-party aggregators (review sites, industry news, casino-data aggregators), none of which were cross-checked against a raw primary-source read. Confidence is capped accordingly. The single most important investigative finding is that the Casumo brand already holds an apparently active, DGOJ-granted Spanish licence via a dedicated entity (Casumo Spain PLC) and a dedicated domain (casumo.es), and that the .com property under investigation appears to carry its own geoblocking infrastructure for restricted markets — a pattern more consistent with a regulated operator maintaining market segregation than with an illegal offshore site targeting Spain. Recommended next steps for the case file, in priority order: (1) perform a geo-located technical check of https://casumo.com/ from a Spanish IP/VPN exit to confirm whether it is actually blocked or in fact reachable and offering Spanish-currency/language content; (2) obtain a primary-source read of the DGOJ operator page and its listed authorised URL(s) for Casumo Spain PLC to confirm casumo.es (not .com) is the licensed domain; (3) if resources allow, query the UK Companies House and Malta Business Registry directly (rather than aggregators) to resolve the Recro Limited jurisdiction/registration-number discrepancy noted above; (4) if casumo.com is confirmed reachable and Spain-targeting from Spain, re-run this assessment as the risk picture would materially change and priority should be revisited upward.
